content.text: When you switch on a light, electric current flows through the circuit almost instantly. But what exactly is electric current? It's the flow of electric charge—typically electrons moving through wires—and understanding it is fundamental to all electrical and electronic technology.
Electric current (I) is the rate of flow of electric charge, measured in amperes (A). The formula is I = Q/t, where Q is charge in coulombs and t is time in seconds.

Despite electrons drifting slowly through wires (often less than 1 mm/s), the electrical signal travels at near the speed of light. This is because the electric field propagates almost instantly, causing all electrons to start moving at roughly the same time.
— Current is the same entering and leaving a component. Energy is transferred, not charge.
"Electrons move at the speed of light"
— Electrons drift slowly (~0.1 mm/s). The electric field propagates quickly.
"Current flows from positive because that's where the charge comes from"
— Conventional current is a historical convention. Electrons actually flow from negative to positive.
— Higher current can mean more electrons moving, not necessarily faster electrons.
— Ammeters must be in series. Connecting in parallel would short-circuit the component.

In a series circuit, current is the same at all points. (recall)

An ammeter is connected in series, so all current must pass through it. If it had high resistance, it would reduce the current in the circuit and give a lower, inaccurate reading. Ideally it has zero resistance so it does not affect the circuit.
